parts.name: n7-drawers (batch n7)
parts.text: Part of the problem is that the Buddha (or the people writing his words down) stored the pieces of the puzzle in different drawers. For instance, he talks about direct sensations as the gateway in Ud 1.10, but explains how contact creates “the world” in a chain in SN 12.44. He talks about how consciousness and mind-and-body are like two bundles of reeds that lean against each other (remove one and the other falls down, Jenga!) in SN 12.67.

parts.name: neighbour of n7-drawers (batch n7): the paragraph before it
parts.text: After 15 years of reading popular & obscure Buddhist books, plus countless hours on forums like SuttaCentral.net, I never once found a positive definition of what nibbāna actually is. Everyone says what nibbāna does (liberates), what it ends (rebirth, consciousness, defilements), what it isn’t (anything), and then gives me the aggregates, sense bases, dependent origination, and no-self again. But what was the experience all those lists were pointing to? Why is it that no Theravāda monk ever seems to be clear despite devoting a life to this? In the Buddha’s time, it was common even for laypeople to become stream-enterers and beyond (DN 16).
